analysis.one_liner: Strengthens federal protection against workplace discrimination, with caps and new limits on harassment lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The Senate set the bill aside without a vote in November 1991, after a bipartisan compromise civil rights law was enacted instead.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the Senate Republicans' version of a 1991 civil rights bill responding to recent Supreme Court rulings that had made job discrimination cases harder to win. It would have written a standard into law letting workers challenge employer practices that harm women or minorities even without proof of intent, made workplace harassment itself an illegal practice with new remedies, extended the law to congressional employees, and added filing time and interest awards against the federal government. It also capped harassment awards, required workers to use their employer's internal complaint system first, and encouraged arbitration instead of court. A competing bill passed and was vetoed; a final compromise, containing stronger remedies for workers than this bill, became law instead, and this version was set aside without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face discrimination based on race, sex, religion, or national origin would gain clearer legal standards and new remedies, including monetary awards of up to $150,000 for harassment and emergency court relief while harassment is ongoing. Congressional employees would gain civil rights protections they previously lacked. Workers suing the federal government would get more time to file and interest on delayed payments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of workplace discrimination and harassment

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes a legal standard for 'disparate impact' cases into the Civil Rights Act: a worker can win by showing a practice harms women or minorities and the employer cannot show it is justified by business necessity, even without proving intentional discrimination [S2] [S3].

It makes harassment based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin an unlawful employment practice, lets courts issue emergency relief to stop ongoing harassment, and allows monetary awards of up to $150,000 [S2] [S3].
It extends federal employment discrimination law to the Congress, its committees, and members' offices, giving each House authority to enforce the rules against its own employees [S2] [S3].
It clarifies that the right to make and enforce contracts covers every benefit and term of a contract and is protected against discrimination by private parties as well as state action [S2] [S3].

It extends the filing deadline for federal employees from 30 to 90 days, lets winning plaintiffs recover expert witness fees, and gives the same interest on delayed payments from the government as from private defendants [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the cost: new liability for harassment, a codified disparate-impact standard they would have to justify their practices against, and fee awards. The bill limits that exposure with a $150,000 award cap, a judge rather than jury deciding award amounts, a shield for employers whose internal complaint procedures were not used, and encouragement of binding arbitration.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing discrimination and harassment claims

drawbacks.text: A worker who did not use an employer's internal harassment-complaint procedure within 90 days could lose the right to bring a harassment claim at all, a shield for employers [S3].
Harassment monetary awards are capped at $150,000, and in no case could a jury decide the amount — a judge alone would set it [S3].

The bill defines 'justified by business necessity' loosely, as a practice that an employer's goals are 'significantly served by, even if they do not require' it — a weaker standard for workers than the one in competing versions of the bill [S3].

It encourages binding arbitration instead of court resolution whenever parties agree, which in employment disputes typically pits an individual worker against an employer who chooses the arbitrator repeatedly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given discrimination victims real new remedies, but it was deliberately narrower than the competing Democratic bill: weaker business-necessity standard, capped and judge-set harassment awards, an internal-procedure shield for employers, and a push toward arbitration. It was the employers' side of the 1991 civil rights compromise — meaningful protection, with meaningful limits. The law actually enacted later that year kept the damage caps but let juries hear damages claims and raised the caps with employer size, making it more favorable to workers than this version.

outcome.mechanism: After a compromise civil rights bill negotiated with the White House became law instead, the Senate agreed by unanimous consent to postpone this bill indefinitely, so it never came to an up-or-down vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Dole and eight other Senate Republicans on March 12, 1991, and referred to the Labor and Human Resources Committee [S1] [S3].
On September 24, 1991, the committee was discharged and the bill was placed on the Senate calendar under general orders, meaning it was waiting for floor time [S5].
On November 22, 1991, the Senate indefinitely postponed the bill by unanimous consent, ending its chances without any vote on its merits [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers arguably came out ahead even though this bill died: the compromise Civil Rights Act of 1991 that passed instead was more favorable to workers than this version (jury-determined damages, higher caps tied to employer size, no internal-procedure bar). Employers did better than they would have under the vetoed Democratic bill, which had no damage caps. The broader 1991 fight — President Bush's veto of the Senate-passed bill in October and the subsequent compromise — is well-known history beyond the record for this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, via the stronger compromise law

for.name: Sen. Robert Dole
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as the Republicans' answer to the competing Democratic civil rights bill and later helped negotiate the compromise that became law.

for.name: 10 of 43 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the original group included Hatch, Simpson, McCain, Stevens, Murkowski, Garn, McConnell, and Kasten.

against.name: The Senate
against.what_they_did: Indefinitely postponed the bill by unanimous consent, setting it aside without a vote.

against.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee; sponsor of the competing bill (S. 1745)
against.what_they_did: Sponsored the rival civil rights bill that was the main vehicle; his bill, not this one, became the basis for the law eventually enacted.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the Senate-passed Democratic civil rights bill in October 1991 and pressed for the compromise that replaced both bills.

sides.party_line_note: All ten cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill was the Republican alternative in a civil rights fight that split largely along party lines — though the final law that passed instead was a bipartisan compromise negotiated by senators of both parties.

industries.industry: Employers subject to federal anti-discrimination law
industries.note: The bill creates new harassment liability and codifies the disparate-impact standard, but it also caps harassment awards at $150,000, bars claims from workers who skip the employer's internal complaint procedure, lets judges rather than juries set awards, and encourages arbitration — a package that limits how much employers can be made to pay workers.

industries.industry: Binding arbitration and alternative dispute resolution providers
industries.note: The bill encourages arbitration instead of court resolution of discrimination disputes when parties agree, expanding the role of private arbitration in civil rights cases.

New harassment claims and prevailing-party fee awards, including expert fees up to $300 a day, expand the market for representing discrimination victims — but the arbitration preference and award caps limit that.
